speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head X of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last year, we witnessed the year-long SG50 celebrations which were held to mark the 50th anniversary of our Independence.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is heartening is that about 400 of the initiatives were started by ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Each project was evaluated on its ability to raise awareness of our Singaporean identity, our sense of belonging to Singapore, outreach to engage the community; as well as to show potential in successful completion and execution according to plan.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The ground-up initiatives saw many new innovative projects that rallied Singaporeans together and touched our hearts.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There were many short films and documentaries produced by individuals and groups.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: One such documentary is "And So They Say", a documentary project showcasing an honest narrative on life's construct from interviews with 25 seniors, allowing an intimate glimpse into the legacy of Singapore's Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is an effort to foster a sense of community and belonging.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It features a video collection of stories from Singaporeans and people who have come to call Singapore home.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With food being a favourite Singaporean past-time, there were also projects with a food theme, such as #SgEatWithUs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is a ground-up movement that celebrated the stories and values of Singaporeans surrounding local home-cooked food by building a community which shares, cooks and appreciates local home-cooked food.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There was a series of food carnivals organised to bring people together.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is another project called "jiakSimi.sg", a website documenting recipes of top 50 local hawker dishes from the major races in Singapore, accompanied by a short write-up on each dish's origin, history and where we can find them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These celebrations led Singaporeans to appreciate the Pioneer Generation and the country's past and to reflect on how Singapore overcame the odds.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The variety of activities touched the hearts of many and it helped to bring a sense of belonging and bonding to everyone.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: People were encouraged to come together and build the future together, to share their memories of the past and contribute ideas on what future they want.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many other pieces of feedback were given during dialogue sessions, young people shared their aspirations and these were subsequently captured in The Future of Us exhibition.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, one important discussion dwelt on the need to build on the trust and confidence among different races in the light of challenges posed by religious extremists.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The important point is: now that we have aroused so many good vibes, elicited so much feedback, thoughts and ideas, where do we go from here?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How do we make good use of the goodwill and gems arising from the SG50 celebrations so that we do not miss out on the opportunities to grow and nurture them to take us into the next 50 years?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am glad and excited on the proposed Our Singapore Fund that was announced in this year's Budget.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister shed more light and details on this new fund?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is this a continuation of the SG50 Celebratory Fund?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What valuable lessons have we learnt from the SG50 Celebratory Fund that we can apply to Our Singapore Fund?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will the Government increase the fund size if there is an overwhelming demand?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am confident that the Our Singapore Fund will be welcome and well-utilised.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Global competition will not get any easier and the needs of companies from the workforce are ever-changing.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   MENDAKI's Future Ready Unit comprises members who are experts in their respective fields and they can share their experience to help the community benefit from the national SkillsFuture initiatives.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the tasks of this unit is to identify strategies that can equip Malay/Muslim workers, including students, with the relevant skills, in addition to encouraging Malay/Muslim workers to identify the various pathways that they can take in order to deepen their knowledge in a certain area.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will help them to acquire future skills that are relevant so that they will stay employable when the industries here undergo the transformation to improve productivity and stay competitive.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): I would like to ask the Minister what are some of the plans that the Future Ready Unit will be working on for the coming year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Singapore is gearing itself for the Future Economy that will be challenging and offers many opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There will be structural changes in our economy and this will invariably affect jobs and the skill demands of the workforce among the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Retraining and staying relevant to the needs of the economy are necessary if the workers wish to find jobs and keep pace with the changing economic environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The whole country will have to work hard to stay competitive in the global market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many businesses are jostling for market share with lower profit margins, as they try to retain their clients or even when getting new customers on board.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe our Government will do everything within its means to help Singapore's workforce, including Malay/Muslim workers, to be retrained and to keep them relevant to the Future Economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister outline what is MENDAKI and SENSE College doing to help the various segments of the Malay/Muslim workforce so that they can cope with the short- to medium-term challenges, apart from other national initiatives that are available now?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: This progress was made possible through the efforts of the Government, our Malay/Muslim organisations, families and parents.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: But the world is changing and there are many new challenges.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: As a community, we have to respond to this changing landscape.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: I was a tutor in the flagship MENDAKI tuition scheme (MTS) for many years.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: MTS centre supervisors and tutors play a very critical role in ensuring the success of MTS.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: How can we better support and equip our tutors so that they can ensure even better educational outcomes for our students?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, I will speak in Malay.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   The achievement and progress of our community were made possible through the efforts and dedication of parents and families within our community, as well as the strong support from the Government and Malay/Muslim organisations.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: The Malay/Muslim community in Singapore has undeniably achieved much progress.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: The General Household Survey 2015 report found that the Malay/Muslim community in Singapore is doing better in terms of education, compared to five years ago.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: However, the world is changing and will continue to change.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: On the issue of education, this fund is crucial so that our children can succeed in school and enhance their knowledge in order to have a brighter future.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: We must work with parents, teachers, schools and community leaders so that our children have the opportunity to achieve their potential through education.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: MTS provides tuition classes for subjects like English Language, Mathematics and Science.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: The success of this scheme surely depends on the abilities of its tutors.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Hence, may I know how we can provide better support and equip the MTS tutors with the necessary skills so that they can perform their duty to ensure that our children can excel further in education?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our community has been putting in a lot of effort trying to reduce the disamenities faced by disrupted and reconstituted families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The "Many Helping Hands" approach is certainly helpful towards this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There may be a need to continue to enhance resources, empowerment as well as the take-up rate and regular attendances at counselling and nurturing sessions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Currently, there are some generic as well as targeted programmes for these families that are being offered but we hope that more can come forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Has this proportion remained stable or has it changed over the last three to five years?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I really admire the efforts of the Muslim community in Singapore in the administration of mosques.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The management board and staff of every mosque work hard to run these mosques, while the Muslim community also plays a role to achieve stability for the mosques by contributing their money and energy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As we know, mosques welcome contributions from the community in any shape or form, especially financial contributions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because, as I understand it, all the expenses incurred in running a mosque like utility bills, payment of monthly salaries and so on are also funded with money contributed by the community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This spirit of partnership is born out of the intent and sincere effort to achieve a shared objective that is to help mosques in Singapore prosper.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The stability of mosques, which is built on this spirit of partnership, will turn mosques into one of the important and main contributors not only in spiritual development, but also in the social development of our Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This will also strengthen the spirit of partnership between the Government and Malay/Muslim bodies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Mr Chairman, the numbers of underage and teenage marriages have always been on the radar of our community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This is because observations, studies and statistics have shown a significant proportion of them to have family financial problems, as well as a higher rate of divorce, and subsequent remarriages, resulting in many challenges and disruptions for the children of such families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Efforts have been proactive and have been put forth to contain their numbers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Marriage counselling has also been targeted towards this group of people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How are we tracking them and the existing couples who need assistance and continue to need assistance?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Are there further interventions and new initiatives underway?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam, you can take your three cuts together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Strong families are the foundation of a resilient community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Hence, efforts should be made to help families stay strong.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important for the Government to provide specific programmes to help the community with this, especially for young couples.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are already Marriage Preparation Courses that couples who intend to get married have to attend.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These courses are useful in preparing these couples so that they can receive some guidance and are encouraged to think about the important aspects of marriage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In order to ensure the effectiveness of this programme, a review and assessment should be done to see whether this programme has achieved its objectives and is well-received by couples who attend the courses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, it is also important to ensure that there is a follow-up programme to help couples in the early years of their marriage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They may face challenges when dealing with issues like finances, relations with in-laws, plans for their children and so on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope that attention can be given to this group in order to help them go through the challenging times during their marriage and ensure that they stay together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Strong families are the foundation of a resilient community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is thus important to invest in programmes to help families stay strong.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that there are already in place Marriage Preparation Courses for couples to provide the guidance and support for those who intend to be married.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Apart from these courses, I believe that it is also imperative that we give some support to couples with young children in the early years of their marriage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These couples have to cope with significant changes in their lives and may face some challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Divorce rates have remained steady over the past few years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that the Syariah Court's efforts in conducting counselling programmes have helped.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, usually, couples who go to the Syariah Court would have already decided to proceed with divorce and it is hard to save their marriage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Even so, it is important for us to ensure that their family relationship is preserved, especially if the couple have small children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The couple should discuss in a mature manner and come up with a plan for their children after they are divorced.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Based on my past experience as a lawyer and as the Deputy Registrar at the Syariah Court, divorced couples are usually still angry and have difficulty talking to each other.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This behaviour will have a negative effect on their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Hence, efforts should be taken to provide support for these couples.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Syariah Court has embarked on several initiatives like discussing parenting plans during counselling and information sessions for those who have divorced.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think that there should be a sustained effort in this matter to provide support to couples who are divorcing, in order to take care of their children's well-being.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is also important for counsellors and lawyers who are assisting divorcing couples to be trained and equipped with the necessary skills, so that they can give effective support and guidance to divorcing couples.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Divorce rates have remained steady over the past few years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that the Syariah Court, through its Marriage Counselling Programme, has helped in this regard.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But not all marriages can be saved and the Syariah Court has embarked on several measures to help divorcing couples and to ensure the best interests of the children are met.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have also seen some developments in the Family Justice Courts in respect of child-centric initiatives, such as the introduction of Parenting Coordinators.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Are there plans to mirror some of these developments and, in particular, in enhancing the capabilities of our practitioners, such as lawyers and the marriage counsellors?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Syariah Court is a key institution in the Muslim community, dealing primarily with Muslim divorces.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The powers of the Syariah Court are set out in the Administration of Muslim Law Act (AMLA) and the specific procedures are detailed in the Muslim Marriage and Divorce Rules (MMDR).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Court deals with couples and families and it has, over the years, developed its procedures to enhance its services to the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that efforts can be put in place to further enhance the Court's delivery of services in two areas, namely: (a) through improvements to the Court's processes; and (b) through a review and update of AMLA and MMDR.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, the Court may wish to consider introducing electronic or online filing of Court documents like how it is done in the Family Justice Courts and the State Courts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is also in keeping with the national approach of embracing technology to improve productivity and enhancing service to the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Processes like the registration process can be made simpler and faster and data collected can be stored and used at the next stage of proceedings, without requiring parties to provide the same information again.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important to do so, so that the Court can better serve the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: (In Malay):    Sir, our mosques play an important role in the lives of our community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Our mosques are not only a place where we seek tranquillity, but also a place for us to acquire religious knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Mosques are also the key to a broader network in the provision of social assistance, including zakat, and to refer cases to the Social Service Offices (SSOs) and Family Service Centres (FSCs), if necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: There is a very strong gotong royong spirit in our mosques.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Many youths serve as volunteers in various mosque activities and operations, especially during Friday prayers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened to see such strong support from the community, because everyone in the community has a role to ensure that our mosques are safe and comfortable for all.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   The Joint Madrasah System (JMS) that was implemented in 2009 has come a long way in levelling up our full-time Madrasah education system and developing it into a world-class education system.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many changes have been made to strengthen our Madrasah education, including the revamp of secondary education for Madrasah Al Arabiah, where from 2015, the students are able to choose between a four-year direct GCE "O" Level route; or a five-year GCE "N" Level route, followed by the GCE 'O' Level examinations.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the light of abundant opportunities in the information technology and other growth sectors, I would like to know how our Madrasah curriculum will be modified and strengthened to better prepare our full-time Madrasah students, so that they can seize the available opportunities when they join the workforce.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs if he can provide an update on the progress of the JMS and what else can be done to make our full-time Madrasah system more holistic.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My two other concerns are: firstly, students in our mainstream schools who come from lower-income families can tap on the Ministry of Education (MOE) Financial Assistance Scheme (FAS).

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, for full-time Madrasah students who may come from less privileged or lower-income families, are there similar financial assistance schemes provided by MUIS or the madrasahs?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are concerns in the community about where the Madrasah will be relocated and whether a longer term lease can be obtained, so that proper facilities can be built and implemented for the students and asatizahs of Madrasah Al Arabiah.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: (In Malay):   The religion of a person can play an important role because it is a form of guidance, especially in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is a good sign that more Malay/Muslim youths and adults are actively seeking out a better understanding of Islam.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is evident from the relatively good demand for part-time Islamic Studies in Singapore, from both public and private institutions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: One of the key thrusts of MUIS' fifth three-year plan is to focus on increasing the community's participation in Islamic Education, particularly among our young.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This will help to ensure that our young remain rooted to the proper values, based on the foundations of Islam.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The actions of extremists in the Middle East have generated a lot of curiosity and controversy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Subsequently, there is a prevalence of flawed online resources masquerading as Islamic teachings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: These resources are often dynamic and provocative, and youths who do not have a good understanding of the religion would run the risk of being susceptible to erroneous teachings and become misguided.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: An effective curriculum in Islamic Studies can help to empower a cohesive and progressive Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is important that all institutions offering Islamic Studies provide legitimate curriculum and content that are true to Islam, easily absorbed and understood.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Could the Minister elaborate on plans and strategies for part-time religious education in the coming years?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: This is what makes Singapore united as a nation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: It is the focal point of our national identity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Unfortunately, we are facing challenging times where falsehood is being hailed as the truth and it is becoming increasingly difficult to counter such propaganda.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: As a Muslim, I am worried that people of other faiths may have a biased view of Islam in light of recent events around the world.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: There is an urgent need to counter any possible negative perception.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: We have closed ranks and stood together to speak out against extremism and against those who could threaten our security.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: (In Malay):   Our asatizahs, or religious teachers, can play an important role to discuss the issue of terrorism and also guide our community about life in a multireligious society like ours.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I am heartened to see that many of our asatizahs are aware that it is important that we practise tolerance and give and take with other religious groups.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Hence, in order to play this role better, it is imperative that we provide training for our asatizahs and equip them with secular knowledge that is updated and relevant, so that they have a wider perspective of issues pertaining to society and the world.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Our asatizahs must also possess an open mind and a willingness to acquire the latest secular knowledge in their effort to help the community understand the challenges that can damage a harmonious plural society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Chairperson, I am pleased and proud to see so many of our madrasah students progressing in education, with some of them even going on to achieve excellence in the mainstream schools.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many have also continued their studies in Islamic institutions overseas like Cairo and Jordan.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This group will potentially become future community leaders and, hence, we should continue to engage and communicate with them, so that they will stay rooted here.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The knowledge that they acquire overseas, together with an understanding of the multiracial and socio-economic situation in Singapore, will be crucial.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will MUIS and our religious leaders shape the relationship and ties with this group and how are they being prepared for their return to our shores?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that we can make good use of their potential and ensure that every graduate has ample opportunity to serve our community, religion as well as our economy in the future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Diversity will always be part of our lives, and these young people will also play an important role in maintaining our solidarity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this era, the education of our young is not solely done in schools because we must also expose them to a broader mindset and perspectives, including life values, especially with the influence of social media.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So far, we have been able to increase understanding through various initiatives, but due to the presence of many influences and challenges, including within the Muslim community itself, the situation may be different for future generations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The ability to give and take, and being tolerant, does not happen automatically.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is the Minister's view on the type of life values that our young people should display and advocate and how can we encourage more Malay/Muslim youths to play a part in nation-building and provide leadership opportunities for them in the community as well as at the national level?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Its original role was countering communist activities and fostering social stability and national security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: PA has gone from community centres to community clubs, from providing television sets and simple sports facilities to holding courses and large-scale activities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned with two aspects: the PA's ever-increasing budget and whether PA has, in some respects, deviated from its mandate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, it seems to me that some PA activities have exceeded its mandate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To recap, the People's Association Act states that PA is incorporated for the purpose of promoting community recreation and incidental matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Its objects are stated to relate to fostering cohesion and bonding and to promoting group participation that transcends sectional loyalties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The PA's role then is to unite, receiving heavy taxpayer funding for such.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: PA activists being mobilised to campaign for People's Action Party (PAP) candidates at elections is just one aspect.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I then wrote several times to the CCC, but it seems that my letters do not even merit a reply.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Alex Yam, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, the founding fathers of modern Singapore placed a huge premium on multiculturalism and racial harmony to help chart Singapore's course forward towards success and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But in our journey towards these goals, did we leave behind the resilience that we had in us and which served us so well, when standing up to the communists and communalists in our formative years?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Did our new-found prosperity and confidence in ourselves lead us to losing our fundamental principle of being Singaporeans as one united people?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our children are taught the importance of unity and racial harmony in schools.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But how much of it is retained in their later years?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How big an impact is information gleaned online, so much so that intolerance takes root in our young?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For those who are somewhat surprised by what I have said, I would, however, give in that when we look online, this is the situation that we see.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, art challenges us, inspires us, enables us and provokes us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, Singapore has made tremendous progress in growing, promoting and nurturing a cultural landscape, curating both world-class museums and the performance arts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even as we grow this scene and put in the investments, how do we make sure that just such a landscape is accessible and relevant to Singaporeans and our own local culture?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Accessibility also lies beyond whether art is comprehensible but also whether fundamentally it is physically accessible.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Often, we hear of people talking about visiting the museum, watching the latest theatre production.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But for people with disability, attending a concert is not as simple as buying a ticket and turning up, and going to an exhibition may not be as simple as an impromptu visit to the galleries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, the less fortunate, especially children, deserve a stake in our nascent arts scene.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Arts hold tremendous remarkable learning opportunities for the young, and no one should be left behind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How has the Ministry been tapping on this and what plans does the Ministry have, especially in engaging our youths with arts, heritage and culture?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, in the past decade, we have seen many commendable infrastructure developments to boost our arts and culture scene for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There is an almost inexhaustible number of arts venues listed in the Singapore Art Gallery Guide.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There are also more than 20 heritage centres and museums about history and culture.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Our newly revamped museums with state-of-the-art technology and our National Gallery opened last year were all welcomed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: These cultural infrastructures were significant investments by our Government.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: However, they need to be complemented and supported by programmes that can engage, enhance and excite our public.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Otherwise, they will remain nothing more than just impressive infrastructures.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I am not sure if we are getting the support from the ground that we are targeting.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Are we getting more people involved and engaged in arts and culture or have we hit a plateau?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: But how do we measure the amount of arts activities in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How do we currently stand, compared to five years ago, for instance?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: And how do we stand, compared to other countries?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Artnet, for example, has listed Oslo, Brussels and Mexico City as the best cities for the modern-day artist.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What can we learn from these artistic countries to close the gap and make arts more accessible and pleasurable for Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What does the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) see as the next step, in our efforts to develop our city centre as a lively arts and cultural belt that is distinctively Singaporean, and that Singaporeans can be proud of and enjoy?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Raising the level of appreciation of our traditional arts can help Singaporeans better understand our roots, promote cross-cultural understanding and help make sense of "What does it mean to be Singaporean?" How can MCCY help more young Singaporeans to be exposed to and learn to appreciate traditional arts in schools and forge cross-cultural understanding?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: To support and promote Singapore traditional arts, we need to have greater focus or attention on the development of artistic and management capabilities, as well as to cultivate new audiences across different genres of traditional arts.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We need to identify the training needs of the traditional arts scene, showcase homegrown talents, encourage active cultural and knowledge exchange and provide networking opportunities among artists, both locally and regionally.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: These initiatives will complement the existing total range of support provided for traditional arts groups, ranging from grants and arts house subsidies, to the national competitions to identify and nurture young talents in traditional arts and music.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Where are we now in promoting traditional arts in Singapore today?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Minister give the House an update on the progress?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is especially so when young minds in schools are exposed early to the history of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I am of the view that this can only be achieved if history is presented to encourage students to consider multiple perspectives and engage in critical thinking.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This will also reduce students' and parents' perceptions of using history as Government propaganda.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I believe the same should apply to the representations of history in exhibitions curated by the National Heritage Board (NHB).

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This would include exhibitions at museums such as the National Museum and interpretive centres, such as the Malay Heritage Centre and Nanyang Memorial Hall.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is time we move away from representations of a "standard" or "official" history.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We should allow different interpretations of history with the goal of encouraging critical thinking and promoting citizenship education to guide NHB exhibitions.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: For example, the recent Parliament in Singapore History exhibition could take on different interpretations as seen from the multiple perspectives of the Pioneer statesmen, ruling party backbenchers, opposition party Members, women Members, minority Members and so on.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: NHB now provides grants to organisations and individuals keen to conduct historical research and curate exhibitions on history.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The historical exhibitions will have more legitimacy with the public and, therefore, promote citizenship education.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Our heritage is key to understanding who we are and where we came from.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In the past few years we have seen several public debates over heritage and what we should preserve.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We have also seen several archaeological excavations, for example, in Fort Canning, St Andrew's Cathedral, Adam Park, Cathedral of the Good Shepherd, the site of the National Gallery Singapore and most recently, Empress Place.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: These excavations are signs of our interests in our past and the Government's efforts to support heritage awareness.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Without these assessments, we would not know if such development would put historically significant buildings, structures or artefacts at risk.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: These are assessments that will help URA or the Minister make better informed decisions over development.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun, you have two cuts, you can take them together.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am the Artistic Director of a theatre company that is very much involved in creating and curating socially-engaged and community-engaged art.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am also a member of the examination board of the Intercultural Theatre Institute.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I quote: "...a nation of cultured and graceful people, at home with our heritage, and proud of our Singapore identity".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve this vision, two strategic directions were identified: one, to bring arts and culture to everyone, everywhere, and every day; two, to build capabilities to achieve excellence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This would mean that come 2017, we can look forward to a comprehensive review of what has been achieved.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This review will be an important document to help us determine the approaches we should take for the next eight years as we move into 2025.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence my two cuts will deal with these two strategic directions for the future.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It has increased the number of art activities and brought the arts closer to our doorstep.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This has provided livelihoods for some artists who are very committed to working with the community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, I would like MCCY to look at the following issues.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Initiated by artist Alecia Neo, the project involves seven students living with visual impairment from Ahmad Ibrahim Secondary School.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Over two years, under the guidance of mentors from a diverse range of professions, the students were immersed in a very deep process of discovery, which resulted in them creating works that explore their lives and dreams.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The various artworks now displayed at the gallery comprise music videos about friendship and discrimination, a short film about vulnerability of love and boyhood, a motivational speech, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the motivational talk, student Dallon Au revealed his insecurity as someone with impaired vision, I quote, "Many times, I just feel like giving up and killing myself.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is so unbecoming of a motivational speaker, right?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: You have no idea how many times people have said this to me. ‘If you cannot even keep yourself motivated, how are you going to motivate others?' Believe me, I agree.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But I am working on it and I am getting better." Through the work, you can see how these students had learnt so much about themselves through a highly engaged process facilitated by very thoughtful and sensitive artists and mentors.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The process has resulted in the creation of artworks that are moving and of high quality. "Unseen" is deeply engaging and impactful.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As we move towards the future, we should encourage more of such deep and engaging work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The depth and process will result in profound learning experiences for the community and will also result in artistic work that is aesthetically rich.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It moves the audience, changes their sensibilities, by making the invisible visible and the unheard heard.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Facilitation and organisational skills are specialties that not all artists possess.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Artists need a different set of skills to encourage and inspire community participants to express their creative selves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, artists may need to organise and mobilise resources from different agencies to make projects happen.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if you are going to do a project on end-of-life issues, we may require the involvement of the Agency for Integrated Care, hospitals, nursing homes, caregiver communities, amongst many others.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these agencies are not familiar with arts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, when artists partner them to create community work, dialogue and processes are important so as to avoid miscommunication and distrust.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This requires specialisation, an intermediary role that bridges artists and communities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A good example of such a good intermediary would be the group ArtsWok Collaborative.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They facilitated and produced "The Rite of Spring", a dance performance choreographed by Cultural Medallion recipient Angela Liong of Arts Fission.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The performance was presented at Esplanade Theatre, featured four different elderly groups like AWWA Seniors Activity Centre, AWWA Community Home for Senior Citizens, National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) Eldercare and Henderson Senior Citizens' Home, as well as children.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To accomplish such an intergenerational work, a lot of facilitation and organisation need to be done.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The intermediary needs to be someone who is well-versed in the process of art-making but, at the same time, understands the art of community engagement deeply.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Many artists who work in the community tend to operate as individuals, without the backing of administrative and organisational support.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To bring arts closer to the community, such that it becomes an everyday presence, we should begin looking at creative place-making.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Creative place-paking makes the arts a part of community living.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not a place or venue management.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not about presenting performances and programmes to create buzz.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: According to Tuan Yi Fu, a well-known geographer, a place comes into existence when there is a "moment of pause", which provides people within the space to reflect and connect with others around them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is created not by transactional needs, but by relational needs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In creative place-making, the arts are an essential mediator that helps to bring the community together.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important for artists to want to be involved in place-making; they must want to see community engagement very much as part of their work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Creative place-making will only be sustainable if it is ground-up.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In examining the Ministry's key performance indicators, I noted that there is an emphasis on the instrumentalisation of art: what art can do for society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But I would also like to recall a Chinese saying: 工欲善其事，必先利其器.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That is, to do a good job, the artisan must have the best tool to do it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In this case, the art must be good.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Besides having institutions to provide the best arts education for emerging artists, there must also be arts centres or venues that will help young or mature artists develop their craft without the pressure of market forces.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Institutions that pay attention to developmental objectives must be seen differently from, say, a theatre company that sells tickets to their work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But for institutions with a developmental objective, their focus should be on process over results, experimentation over tried-and-tested products.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, The Substation was a home for the arts, a place for artists to learn, a safe space within which they could venture to explore, that is, to innovate.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Artists like Lee Wen and Amanda Heng created some of their most interesting works there and these artists later became Cultural Medallion recipients, honoured by the nation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Institutions like this, such as Centre 42, Intercultural Theatre Institute and the up-and-coming Traditional Arts Centre, are important in the development of Singapore's arts scene.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I hope there will be more of such centres; and some of them can support interdisciplinary and intercultural experimentation, developing ways of art-making that incorporate science and technology, as well as different kinds of genres and cultures.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Being such a globalised economy and a connector among different regions, we can take advantage of our status to be a facilitator for exploration and exchange.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to advocate for such institutions to have a different funding model.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The very fact that we have a Ministry and affiliated agencies that look specifically at the arts and what it can do for society means that the arts and politics are not strange bedfellows.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the arts should be viewed for its intrinsic worth, and not merely to serve political purpose.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I think it is apt for me to quote from the great author Lu Xun who spoke about the relationship between arts and politics, I will say this in Mandarin, but I will translate later. "…两者之间，倒有不安于现状的同一。惟政治是要维持现状，自然和不安于现 状的文艺处在不同的方向......政治想维系现状使它统一，文艺催促社会进化 使它渐渐分离…" That is to say, while the arts and politics are frequent fellow travellers because both seek change, at some point on this journey, they will take divergent paths.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is in the nature of art to examine change, to pursue truth.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, art may raise uncomfortable questions, and may seem to divide, but it is through these questions that society can progress.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, MCCY has been very supportive in promoting arts in the community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These activities have added much vibrancy and inclusiveness in our community where arts and culture become more accessible to everyone, everywhere and every day.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I wish to ask the Ministry whether it will continue to promote community arts by providing more funding support to CACCs in the community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Arts streets are often found in important towns and cities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is a place where local artists frequent, display their arts craft and engage the local community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Bukit Panjang Arts Street will not only promote arts and culture.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will also generate greater vibrancy in the community and be a pride of place for our residents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: One day, the Bukit Panjang Arts Street in the heartland may find a place on the Singapore tourist map.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Chairman, our Singaporean children are our gems and the hope for the nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We should endeavour towards making their education and development holistic.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I trust we can all agree that the education and development for the young are not limited to what is taught in school and through the school curriculum.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is our duty to make available as many learning opportunities as possible for our children so that they may be able to gain experience and exposure in different fields and grow up to be well-rounded individuals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One aspect of this learning journey must be exposure to the arts and culture.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Early exposure to the arts and culture helps develop creativity, a strong sense of aesthetics and confidence in children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It also helps sustain their interest and appreciation for culture into adulthood.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In the local context, this learning journey also serves as a platform for them to understand and appreciate the different cultures in Singapore and build their national identity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I also believe that the arts and culture should be made accessible to all children, including those from lower-income families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This endeavour could be a social leveller as all students, regardless of social background, are given the knowledge and exposure that contribute towards their holistic development.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am, therefore, of the view that there should be targeted efforts on the part of the Ministry to reach out to students and families with children to promote interest in the arts and culture.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I would, therefore, like to find out more about the existing programmes that are in place for students and families and the Ministry's plans to reach out to this group.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Whenever there is such news reported in the media, do you know what is the reaction of my residents?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These new households will consist mainly of young adults and young families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They will have a very large demand for sporting facilities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Already, our existing facilities are not enough to cope with the population.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Residents are finding it difficult to have access to their favourite venues and sports on a regular basis.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yishun urgently needs more sports facilities and in greater variety.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is only one swimming complex to serve the entire Yishun Town.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It has only three pools which consist of one competition pool, one teaching pool and one wading pool.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, Queenstown, which has about 20,000 fewer residential units, has a swimming complex with five pools.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On top of that, residents told me that the pool is very rundown.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When they go swimming with their friends and relatives in other parts of Singapore, they feel very envious of the beautiful and modern swimming pools elsewhere.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They look forward to water play facilities like those in Jurong East Swimming Pool.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have been bringing up this request for a few years.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Yishun Swimming Complex urgently needs to be refurbished, redesigned and expanded.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister clarify if there are any plans, especially for the swimming complex?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, I hope that the next big announcement on sporting facilities will be for Yishun.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, first of all, I would like to echo Er Dr Lee's sentiments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I think we can all agree that sports are important.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Sports keep us fit and bring our people together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Sports are also fun and helps us to relax after a long day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But we also live in a fast-paced society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And when we start work, start a family and embark on other transition points in life, it is not easy for us to continue our passion for sports because of life's many demands.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Moving forward, it will be good if MCCY and SportSG can finetune our programmes to ensure a continuum of quality opportunities for Singaporeans to participate more actively in sports.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to hearing from MCCY about the latest developments in these areas.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as the Deputy President of the Singapore Table Tennis Association (STTA).

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: How would NYSI support athletes within and outside SSP?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It indicates that its mission is in the four functional areas of Talent Identification and Development, Coaching, Sports Science and Athlete Life Management.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: How will these functional areas benefit young sportsmen and women?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: In addition, what role would NYSI play in relation to the National Sports Associations?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: For example, STTA runs a Junior Development Squad with student-athletes from mainstream schools as well as those in the School Within School programme, a collaboration that STTA has with SSP.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Will both groups have equal access to NYSI?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Given all of this support, it seems like a wonderful time to pursue a sporting career.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While facilities and Government support are in abundance, have Singaporean attitudes towards sports really changed over the years?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Do parents see a sporting career as a viable, respectable career goal?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Are Singaporean parents going to be "sporting" about their child choosing football, swimming or table tennis over medicine, law and banking?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This is a very real scenario that parents face today, a logical next step in a nation that has invested billions of dollars in world-class facilities and programmes.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I think that more can and needs to be done to address the way people, particularly parents, think about sports.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I know of parents who send their children for intensive coaching to get them into elite schools through the Direct School Admission (DSA) programme, and how these children end up hating the sport they gained direct admission for, as it is not their passion but they are forced into it.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: How many of these children admitted into DSA schools actually continue to pursue the sport beyond school/junior college/polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, at the Sports School, what has become of all the fantastic young talents unearthed during the 2010 Youth Olympic Games?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I remember how the whole country came together to cheer on the boys in the national under-16 football team and how we were all mesmerised by their sheer passion and talent.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Are these boys still together as a team or have they given up on their passions to pursue what would be considered "normal careers" in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But there are children who yearn to pursue a professional career in a sport that they are very good in.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a way the Singapore community, from parents, grandparents, teachers and opinion leaders, can be moved to a point where we see a career footballer or golfer with as much societal value and respect as you would an airline pilot or an architect?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There is nothing wrong with kids pursuing their passion for sports.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We should let them live their dreams and support them to the fullest.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Society should not stigmatise a child who wants to pursue a sports career, regardless of whether the child ultimately makes it or not.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When children are passionate about their dreams, are willing to be disciplined, hardworking and focused to achieve their goals, they are already displaying qualities that any parent should be proud of.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: On the flipside, we should avoid over-coaching children to the point where they lose the love for sports.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Sports should be about passion, fun and joy!

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, what happens when your child says he wants to be a professional footballer?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Well, after the initial alarm, periods of insomnia, and long heart-to-heart conversations, we told our son that he has our fullest support.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: To build a strong sporting spirit, and a sporting nation, parents and society at large need to learn how to be good sports, too.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, SG50 was notable for many things, not least the Southeast Asian (SEA) Games and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Para Games.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Then, we saw the entire country come together as one family to support our national athletes who truly did us proud.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, one enduring memory of that period was when the entire country almost seemed to sing our National Anthem a capella after the sound system failed at one of the venues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have seen how our athletes have inspired a palpable sense of national pride in Singaporeans through these Games, often at great personal sacrifice.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Melvin Yong, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our para-athletes trained hard and competed with international para-athletes of outstanding calibre.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Backed by strong support from our fellow Singaporeans, our para-athletes achieved an outstanding medal haul at the Games.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I was at the National Stadium for the deciding football match between Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Both teams were competing for the bronze medal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singaporeans of all ages were cheering their hearts out in support of Team Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What moved me deeply was the determination shown by our para-athletes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Despite their physical challenges, they displayed grit and resilience.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of them are residents of Tanjong Pagar GRC.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The stadium shook when Mr Muhammad Mubarak scored the winning goal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is so much potential for disability sports to flourish in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The task at hand would be to keep on encouraging participation, as well as to identify, groom and support potential talents so that, one day, we will have a stronger team of para-athletes to represent our country in disability sports.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, Singapore hosted the 28th SEA Games and the 8th ASEAN Para Games.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In both sporting events, our athletes created history by winning a record number of medals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their historic achievements brought the nation together in celebration.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Organising such major events and making sure everything runs smoothly and according to plan are no easy feat.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thankfully, there were thousands of volunteers who responded to the call for help and sacrificed their time to ensure that all aspects of the Games went smoothly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We witnessed a sense of camaraderie among these volunteers, who hail from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Friendships were forged over the months of working and training together, and many of the volunteers have continued to stay in touch with one another since.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To build on this momentum, I would like to ask: what will MCCY be doing to encourage more Singaporeans from various backgrounds to participate or volunteer at sporting events or activities?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Besides volunteering in sporting events, are there plans to extend this to the arts and heritage communities as well?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Work and family commitments prevent many volunteers from continuing, let alone putting in more involvement or time.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a pity because there is an ever-increasing need for more volunteers in our society.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The social needs of the society are plentiful in our ageing population.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: As we progress socio-economically as a country, we need to uplift our lowest income strata groups, such as the less-advantaged families and children.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is necessary for us to better care for them, and this requires more social workers and volunteers.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Befriender volunteers do prevent the seniors from isolation and depression by visiting them in their homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Befriender volunteers are useful in keeping seniors healthier by reminding them to take their medicines, taking them for medical check-ups or early treatment before illnesses get worse.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Although I agree that volunteers are altruistic individuals, I would like to suggest that we do more to recognise them and motivate them to stick with their volunteerism.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The reimbursements are for transport and meal allowance in the course of their roles.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The growth of volunteerism cannot be left to chance alone.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us take whatever steps are necessary to expand and sustain volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to touch on the Singapore Roadmap for Corporate Giving.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Many of us would agree that Singaporeans are a generous people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I would also like to add that many business owners and corporations I have come across have a heart to give.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: There is, of course, more we can do to make Singapore an even more caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: So, I am heartened to hear that MCCY and the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre (NVPC) started developing a Singapore Roadmap for Corporate Giving.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Such a roadmap will provide much needed clarity to employers, employees and voluntary welfare organisations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: How will it help companies, including small and medium enterprises (SMEs), to do more to encourage employer-organised volunteerism?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, fellow Members of Parliament, the Government has rolled out tax incentives to encourage enterprises to do more charitable work and set up the "Our Singapore Fund" to promote social cohesion and a caring spirit.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, many enterprises, including SMEs, do actively participate in all kinds of charitable activities, except that these were not widely publicised by the media.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: By introducing tax incentives, the Government is endorsing the charitable work by enterprises.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, this could enable enterprises to do even more.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Companies which organise charitable activities can "kill two birds with one stone".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Staff who work in different departments do not usually have the chance to interact with other colleagues.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Participating in charitable activities organised by the company gives them the chance to work together and deepen understanding.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, when companies plan for such activities, it would be more effective if they could take reference from some successful experiences.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I would urge the relevant agency to provide cases of some successful corporate social responsibility projects as a reference point.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: While companies could learn by example more easily, charitable organisations would also stand to benefit.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Joan Pereira, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Clearly, there is room for our companies to increase volunteer opportunities for their staff.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Businesses are an important part of our community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By contributing to good causes together with their staff, they build goodwill and gain respect from the public and their customers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their employees also have better job satisfaction and a stronger sense of corporate identity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many employees I have come across admire corporate leaders who have the heart to give back to society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have many examples of corporates contributing money, time and effort to good causes, such as Singapore Airlines (SIA), Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) and Mediacorp.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my constituency, Mr Peter Ng of Sin Kian Choon Fruits Trading is a good example of a business owner from Bukit Merah who has stepped forward to help needy residents in my constituency.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He not only sponsors the fruits and rations for needy households, but helps out in the distribution, too.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For these big companies and SMEs, the employees share with me that they gain great satisfaction seeing the happy and appreciative faces of the residents who received help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, studies have shown a positive association between volunteering and mental, physical and social well-being.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An example of a senior volunteer is Mdm Doh, aged 70, who has been a long-time volunteer with Thong Kheng Welfare Services, Lions Befriender and the RC in Bukit Merah View in my Division.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She has learnt that many elderly value, above all, relational connections – a listening ear, a shoulder to lean on.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She had to respond to a few emergencies and gained great satisfaction in being able to help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, some, especially those who are just starting out as new volunteers, may face challenges in volunteering.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, they may have difficulty in getting a good match between their skills or interests and the segments of need and, most challenging, balancing family and personal commitments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are also some volunteers who cannot find a good fit with the volunteer host organisations or who find that their volunteering experience could have been better managed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are MCCY's plans in managing our pool of talented and active volunteers?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there a portal or a point of contact where they can go to and register their interests and expertise, and be matched to appropriate volunteer host organisations?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After registration, are there volunteer consultants they can turn to for advice and guidance?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And, finally, for areas which need sustainable pools of volunteers so that they can be rostered for their duties, is there a system to organise them?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, Sir, I applaud the Government for its continuing efforts to promote a spirit of charity and volunteerism in our society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To encourage giving by wealthy individuals in Singapore, we should review the laws governing the setting up of charitable trusts by Singapore Citizens and residents.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Often, these persons do not wish to be associated with any conspicuous, high-profile foundation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While these philanthropists have the option to register their charities as "Qualifying Grant Makers", ostensibly subject to "lighter touch" supervision by the Commissioner of Charities, but even this "lighter touch" option is comparatively unattractive, because traditional offshore jurisdictions, such as the Channel Islands and the Caribbean, do not impose such requirements that incur additional administrative costs which eat into the net proceeds which were intended for their beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I do not have actual figures, anecdotal evidence from my interactions with the private trust industry suggests this "shrinkage" is quite significant.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This includes being prohibited from soliciting public funds and ensuring that all gains and income are reserved for charitable causes only.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To qualify, the charitable trust must be administered by a Singapore-licensed trust company to ensure strict governance and regulatory oversight by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Expertise built up in this sector can help Singapore develop yet another global centre of excellence, this time, in a field that connects those who cannot help themselves with those who can and want to help them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And we will do well by doing good.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is that these two fundamental principles are not being effectively passed down to our youths and this gap is showing up in the kind of conversations, or lack of conversations, they are having about religion in society.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A lot of our public education efforts at the school and grassroots levels are still mostly modelling the form of religious tolerance rather than the substance of religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Checking out different places of worship and sharing religious meals during religious festivals are just the tip of the iceberg.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What lies underneath is a far more complex conversation about our beliefs on relationships, life, death, time, work, money, power and more that we need to learn to talk about and listen to.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, we have Social Studies and Civic Moral Education, but many youths will tell you few teachers want to discuss race and religious issues in depth.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many teachers deliberately keep discussions at the surface level because they are scared that the answers could be offensive and get them into legal trouble.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not model for our youths what respectful conversation about religion looks like, someone arbitrarily and potentially dangerous will fill the gap for us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It could be a fundamentalist thought leader, a bigoted website or just prejudiced, ill-informed peers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In some sense, Religious Knowledge (RK) has never been taken out of schools.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It has been ongoing, except everyone is managing it by themselves and cherry-picking their own curriculum and their own teachers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And there are definitely echo chambers forming within exclusionary religious and non-religious communities online and offline.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not teach our young people how to build bridges, they will naturally build walls.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A faith-and-reason programme could have three key characteristics that distinguish it from the old RK programme.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: First, it is not about understanding religion in isolation but understanding why preserving freedom of religion and preserving the secularity of the state both matter to the common good.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Real-life Singapore case studies of clashes between different ideologies, like the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) saga should be discussed and the different stakeholders' responses respectfully debated over.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
